clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia mapped to chromosome 13q14 and originally delineated in a consanguineous kindred; parental consanguinity should raise suspicion.
Typically presents in childhood as spastic paraparesis that may progress to a spastic tetraparesis with age.
Pseudobulbar signs - spastic dysarthria, an exaggerated jaw jerk and emotional lability - are a recognised feature that helps distinguish it within the recessive HSP group.
The causative gene at the SPG24 locus has not been confirmed, so diagnosis is clinical and supported by linkage or exclusion of other loci.
Brisk reflexes and extensor plantar responses with relatively preserved sensation typify the more pure end of the spectrum.
Bladder involvement, chiefly urinary urgency, may develop as the disease advances.
Consider it within the differential of early-onset autosomal recessive HSP alongside SPG27 and SPG28.
There is no disease-modifying treatment; care is symptomatic, with spasticity control and physiotherapy.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG24 is an autosomal recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia linked to chromosome 13q14, first defined in a consanguineous family in whom homozygosity mapping localised the locus. The pathological hallmark shared with the HSP family is a length-dependent distal axonopathy of the corticospinal tracts, but in SPG24 the corticobulbar fibres are also clinically involved, producing pseudobulbar features such as spastic dysarthria and exaggerated jaw and facial reflexes. The specific gene and protein at the SPG24 locus remain unidentified, so the molecular pathway is not established; by analogy with other recessive HSPs it is presumed to involve a housekeeping process essential to the maintenance of long central motor axons, for example axonal transport, lipid or endosomal membrane handling, or mitochondrial function. Childhood onset together with recessive, frequently consanguineous, inheritance distinguishes it clinically from the dominant pure HSPs such as SPG3A and SPG4.
additionalDifferentials: SPG27 and SPG28 - sibling autosomal recessive early-onset subtypes
SPG7 (paraplegin) - a common recessive HSP, sometimes with cerebellar or ocular signs
SPG11 (spatacsin) - recessive HSP typically with a thin corpus callosum and cognitive decline
SPG16 - X-linked complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia
Spastic diplegic cerebral palsy or bilateral perinatal insult - non-progressive pseudobulbar presentation
Dopa-responsive dystonia - a treatable mimic of childhood spastic gait
Arginase deficiency and other metabolic causes of spastic paraparesis
additionalInvestigations: MRI of brain and spinal cord to exclude structural and demyelinating disease and to look for a thin corpus callosum suggesting SPG11
Autozygosity mapping and next-generation sequencing HSP gene panels, especially in consanguineous pedigrees
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography for any associated peripheral neuropathy
Speech and swallow assessment to characterise pseudobulbar involvement
Metabolic screen including very-long-chain fatty acids, plasma amino acids and ammonia
Urodynamic assessment where bladder symptoms are present
redFlags: Rapid progression or a sensory level suggesting a compressive or structural cord lesion
Lower motor neuron or bulbar wasting suggesting motor neuron disease rather than pseudobulbar HSP
Prominent cerebellar or extrapyramidal signs pointing to an alternative diagnosis
Cognitive regression suggesting a broader neurometabolic or neurodegenerative disorder
reference.prognosis: The disorder is slowly progressive from childhood, and ambulation is often maintained with aids for a prolonged period. Pseudobulbar involvement adds to the overall disability, and no curative therapy is available.
pitfalls: Confusing pseudobulbar spastic dysarthria with a primary speech or language disorder
Failing to recognise consanguinity as a pointer to autosomal recessive HSP
Expecting a positive single-gene test, as the SPG24 gene is unconfirmed
Overlooking overlapping subtypes such as SPG11 and SPG7 that do have specific genetic tests
references: Neurogenetics reference literature on hereditary spastic paraplegia
Hereditary spastic paraplegia classification and review articles
management: No gene-directed therapy exists; treat spasticity with oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine and focal botulinum toxin, with intrathecal baclofen for refractory upper- and lower-limb tone
Physiotherapy, stretching, orthoses and seating/rehabilitation support as paraparesis progresses to spastic tetraparesis
Speech and language therapy and swallow assessment for pseudobulbar spastic dysarthria, with aspiration precautions
Consider pharmacotherapy for pseudobulbar emotional lability
Treat urinary urgency with antimuscarinic agents alongside urological review
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, with carrier testing and discussion of consanguinity-related recurrence risk
Escalate to multidisciplinary neurology as bulbar and respiratory involvement advances
